strengths: Timely and novel problem framing: 'token sample complexity' characterizes how a fixed, already-trained attention map converges as the number of context tokens grows at inference — a distinct and relevant question given the push toward very long contexts, cleanly separated from classical (training) sample complexity.

Non-trivial theoretical machinery: the uniform-convergence result (Thm 4.2) combines symmetrization, a vector-valued Dudley entropy integral, and covering-number/Lipschitz/envelope control, while the moment result (Thm 5.3) uses a tail-splitting plus radius-optimization argument to trade the exponential-in-R constant for an explicit dependence on the attention horizon H and coupling Psi.

The hardmax analysis (Prop 5.5) is clean and interpretable: via extreme-value theory it yields a 1/sqrt(log n) rate driven by a Gaussian cancellation effect, which is a genuinely interesting qualitative prediction.

Empirical support is reasonably broad: synthetic Gaussian experiments show good agreement with the predicted horizon-dependent exponents (Fig. 2), and BigBird-RoBERTa experiments across multiple Wikipedia languages and CC-News reveal systematic sub-parametric slowdown that tracks horizon and anisotropy (Figs. 3-4, 6-7).

Good scholarly positioning: the related-work discussion is thorough and honestly contrasts the work with the concurrent Boursier & Boyer paper, clarifying the (dependent Q/K/V) self-attention setting and the moment-vs-L2 distinction as the novel elements.
weaknesses: The statement of the main moment theorem is internally inconsistent and partly circular. The condition 'n >= 4(1/delta - 1) n^{1/8}' is self-referential, and the stated beta = 1/(2(1+32 Psi)) does not match the exponent derived in the proof (1/(2(1+(1/22)Psi))); further different constants appear in Cor. C.4 (32 Psi) and Prop. C.6 (16 Psi). This inconsistency across main results undermines confidence in the exact statements.

Tightness is not established (acknowledged), and the experiments actually validate a different, Gaussian-specific conjectured rate (Thm C.4, beta_th = 1/(2(1+Psi))) rather than the general Theorem 5.3. Consequently the repeated claim that the experiments 'confirm our predictions' overstates the link between theory and evidence.

Real-data methodology is questionable for a 'convergence to the infinite-token limit' claim: the limit is approximated by a finite reference of N_max ~ 5e5 tokens, so measured error is relative to an empirical reference that itself has finite-n bias, which can distort slow-rate estimates. In addition, i.i.d. subsampling from a single long sequence destroys the sequential dependence of language that the theory (correctly) assumes away, so the real-data results only indirectly support the theory.

Experimental details are inconsistent: the text states subsample sizes n in [1000, 3000], whereas Figure 4 reports n up to roughly 3e4, and the reference size N_max is described only approximately. Such inconsistencies hinder reproducibility.

The uniform-convergence bound carries an exponential constant e^{8 R^2 ||Sigma^{1/2} A||_2^2}; the authors themselves concede it is 'essentially useless in practice' for large R, which materially limits the reach of the first main result.

The hardmax result (Prop. 5.5) is restricted to d=1 Gaussian tokens, and the interpretation of why real token embeddings deviate from the 1/sqrt(log n) saturation (skewness/kurtosis/anisotropy) is speculative rather than demonstrated.

The key quantity H (and Psi) used throughout is defined via the unknown data covariance Sigma and the attention matrix A, but for real models neither the true Sigma nor a clear operational estimator is given, making the theoretical predictor hard to test directly on real data (the paper acknowledges no explicit A, Sigma dependence for unknown token distributions).

strengths: Timely and well-motivated question. Framing the convergence of a fixed attention layer as the number of context tokens grows as a 'token sample complexity' problem is natural, and the measure-theoretic/mean-field formulation (attention as an operator on probability measures) is clean and consistent with prior work.

Theorem 4.2 is a genuine technical contribution: obtaining an explicit, uniform (over a ball B_R) convergence rate for the self-attention ratio via symmetrization plus Dudley's chaining, while handling the fact that queries, keys, and values are drawn from the same token set, is non-trivial and is the hardest part of the analysis.

The anisotropy-aware sub-Gaussian modeling (Definition 4.1, attention horizon H = ||Sigma^{1/2} A||_2, coupling Psi = ||Sigma||_2 H^2) is a reasonable attempt to move beyond crude compact-support assumptions and to explain why convergence slows down for ill-conditioned token distributions.

The hardmax result (Proposition 5.5) is elegant and, as far as I can check, correct: the reduction of the empirical attention mean to (M_n^+ + M_n^-)/2, the Gumbel/logistic limit from extreme-value theory, E|G_+-G_-| = ln 4 and Var = pi^2/3, giving the 1/sqrt(ln n) rate, all check out.

Experiments are run not only on synthetic Gaussians but also on a real sparse-attention model (BigBird-RoBERTa) across multiple languages/domains, and the qualitative trend (larger horizon -> slower convergence) is displayed.
Limitations are discussed honestly: the authors state that tightness of the bound in the Gaussian setting is open, that the upper bound is loose, and that the theory assumes i.i.d. tokens.
weaknesses: The headline result (Theorem 5.3) is an upper bound that is explicitly not tight, and its exponent beta = 1/(2(1+32 Psi)) is a proof artifact rather than a meaningful quantity: the constant 32 comes from the sub-Gaussian tail constant c = 1/4 and the exponent 8 in Theorem 4.2. The specific formula therefore carries no intrinsic information, which undercuts the claim that it 'better captures real-data behavior.'

There is a direct inconsistency between the theorem and the experimental validation. Theorem 5.3 gives beta = 1/(2(1+32 Psi)), but Figure 2 and the caption of the Gaussian experiments use beta_th = 1/(2(1+Psi)) (Corollary C.4 itself is written as 1/(2(1+delta2 Psi)), and Proposition C.6 as 1/(2(1+16 Psi))). The formula actually compared against the data (1/(2(1+Psi))) is stated in Proposition C.5/C.20 but is never derived in the appendix. Thus the 'experiments confirm our predictions' claim is not backed by a proven prediction.

The experimental validation is weak. Power-law exponents are fit over n in [1000, 3000] (a factor of 3) using a log-log regression, which is far too narrow to reliably identify a scaling exponent. The reference 'limit' nu is itself a finite empirical distribution of ~5x10^5 tokens, so the measured 'error' is the deviation from an empirical estimate, not from the true infinite-token limit. On real data the theory is only matched qualitatively: with H ~ 20-60 in Figure 3, the predicted beta would be essentially 0, whereas observed exponents are ~0.3-0.5, and this quantitative mismatch is not discussed.

Presentation quality is poor and impedes verification. Examples: the statement of Theorem 4.2 is garbled ('q_{(...)} := 1' repeated), the abstract says softmax approaches 'a hardness' (hardmax), the validity condition is written as n >= 4(1/delta - 1) n^{1/8} in one place and n >= 4(1 - 1/delta) n^{1/8} in Corollary C.4, the proof of Theorem 5.3 reports 1/22 where the theorem says 32, Proposition A.7 is cited where Lemma A.7 is meant, and notation mixes t X with <Ax,X> between the 1-D and d-dimensional derivations.

Conceptual gaps limit relevance to the motivating setting. The entire measure-theoretic framework rests on permutation equivariance, but real Transformers (including BigBird, used in the experiments) employ positional encodings that break it. The i.i.d.-token assumption is also far from correlated text, and the analysis covers a single attention layer with fixed parameters, so the connection to actual long-context multi-layer models is asserted rather than established.

The optimization for R* drops the C sqrt(d) correction in the sub-Gaussian tail bound (Lemma B.14 uses P(||X|| > R) <= exp(-c(R/sigma - C sqrt d)^2)), effectively assuming R/sigma >> C sqrt d. In high dimension (e.g. d = 768 for BigBird) this hidden approximation is not justified and can materially change the derived scaling.

Novelty is limited relative to concurrent and prior work. The mean-field view of attention is established (Sander et al. 2022; Geshkovski et al. 2024/2025; Castin et al. 2025), and Boursier & Boyer (2025) independently study token sample complexity; the stated differentiators (shared vs. independent QKV, moments vs. L^2 error) are incremental, and the covariance/mean corollaries are simple variations of the same argument.

strengths: Novel and timely framing: the paper introduces 'token sample complexity' as the rate at which finite-n attention converges to its infinite-token mean-field limit, cleanly distinguishing it from classical PAC sample complexity. This is well motivated by the trend toward very long context windows and addresses a genuinely under-explored asymptotic regime.

Theorem 4.2 provides a quantitative uniform convergence bound for the attention map on balls B_R, with explicit constants. Extending Dudley's entropy integral to the vector-valued, self-attention setting where queries, keys, and values are drawn from the same token set (introducing autocorrelation) is a non-trivial technical contribution, and the proof sketch (symmetrization + chaining) and detailed appendix support the claim.

Theorem 5.3 and its corollaries refine moment convergence to depend polynomially (rather than exponentially) on the scale via the sub-Gaussianity parameter Sigma, explicitly capturing token anisotropy through the coupling coefficient Psi = ||Sigma||_2 H^2. This is a meaningful improvement over the compact-support analysis and gives interpretable structure to the slowdown.

Proposition 5.5 is an elegant, self-contained result: in the hardmax limit for Gaussian tokens, an exact 1/sqrt(ln n) rate emerges from a symmetry-driven cancellation of the sample max and min, connected to Gaussian extreme value theory. This is a surprising and interesting finding that plausibly explains the extreme slowdown regime.

The empirical work spans both synthetic Gaussian data (across horizons and dimensions) and real BigBird-RoBERTa models on seven datasets/languages, consistently showing sub-parametric rates that degrade systematically with the effective horizon, matching the qualitative prediction of the theory.

Reproducibility is reasonable: code is open-sourced, the protocol (subsampling, Monte Carlo, log-log fitting) is described, and the limitations section honestly states that tightness of the bound remains open and that identifying tight distribution-dependent rates is future work.
weaknesses: The central sub-Gaussian theorem (5.3) contains a large, effectively arbitrary constant (beta = 1/(2(1+32 Psi))), and the authors explicitly acknowledge that tightness is not established. More seriously, there is an internal inconsistency: the proof concludes with exponent 1/(2(1 + (1/22) Psi)) while the theorem states 32 Psi. This discrepancy between the stated result and its derivation undermines confidence in the constant and should be resolved.

There is a mismatch between what the general theorem proves and what the experiments validate. The general bound scales as 1/(2(1+32 Psi)), whereas the Gaussian-specific result (Prop. C.5/C.20) and the experiments use 1/(2(1+Psi)). Thus the headline theorem is not the quantity empirically confirmed; the 'confirmation' pertains to the sharper Gaussian rate, which weakens the claim that the theory 'matches real-data behavior'.

The real-data experiments fit power laws over n in [1000, 3000] only (a factor of ~3), with the mean error in Figure 4 varying by only ~10-20% across the range. Power-law exponents estimated over such a narrow dynamic range are fragile, and the agreement with theory could be partly an artifact of the fit window. A wider range of n (or explicit slope confidence intervals) would strengthen the evidence.

The theory assumes i.i.d. tokens, but the real-data experiments operate on sequential, highly dependent text. The manuscript acknowledges this, yet it means the real-data results do not actually test the theory's assumptions; the suggestion that 'similar convergence behavior may persist' under dependence is speculative rather than demonstrated.

Several presentation issues reduce clarity: the constant q_{(Sigma,A,V,R,d,delta)} in the statement of Theorem 4.2 is garbled in the manuscript, Corollary C.4 contains a sign error (4(1 - 1/delta) n^{1/8}), and the self-referential condition n >= 4(1/delta - 1) n^{1/8} is stated awkwardly. These make the formal statements harder to verify.

For compactly supported distributions the bound's constant grows exponentially in R and is conceded to be 'essentially useless in practice'; even the refined result provides only upper bounds whose exact rate is distribution-dependent, limiting the practical guidance the paper can offer for choosing context lengths.

strengths: Introduces a well-motivated and genuinely new notion—"token sample complexity"—that isolates the inference-time regime (fixed trained parameters, growing context length n) and cleanly distinguishes it from classical PAC/learning-theoretic sample complexity.

Provides explicit, quantitative convergence results with interpretable dependence on token geometry (Σ) and attention parameters (A): Theorem 4.2 (uniform convergence of the attention map), Theorem 5.3 (sub-parametric moment rates O(n^{-β}), β = 1/(2(1+32H²))), and the covariance/MSE/deep-composition corollaries.

The 'attention horizon' H = ||Σ^{1/2}AΣ^{1/2}||₂ is a clean, well-interpreted quantity (largest query–key score in the Mahalanobis unit ball) that organises the theory and connects to practice; the minimization over B yielding H² as the optimal ρ_B is a nice touch.

The hardmax analysis (Proposition 5.5) with the Gaussian symmetry-driven cancellation and the exact 1/√(ln n) rate is an elegant, non-obvious result, complemented by a heavy-tailed counterexample (App. C.9) showing sub-Gaussianity is necessary rather than technical.

The theoretical development is comprehensive (uniform convergence, moments, covariance, MSE, deep stacks, compact-support and Gaussian refinements) and the proofs use standard, appropriate machinery (symmetrization, Dudley chaining, truncation/tail balancing).

Empirical work spans synthetic Gaussians, real text (BigBird, BERT, multiple languages/domains), and an end-to-end downstream task, and it also tests structured (windowed/hybrid) sampling, showing the slowdown is not an artifact of i.i.d. subsampling.
Limitations are discussed honestly (tightness left open, i.i.d. assumption, exponential constants in R).
weaknesses: The bounds are loose in the regimes that matter most. Theorem 4.2's constant grows as e^{8R²||Σ^{1/2}A||²}, and the sub-Gaussian moment rate uses 32H² while the Gaussian refinement (Prop. D.23) uses H². For the reported real-data horizons (H ≈ 35–140), β = 1/(2(1+32H²)) is essentially 0 (≪10^{-3}), whereas the observed exponents are ≈0.25–0.5; thus the bound does not quantitatively 'describe' real-data rates, and the claim that it does (Conclusion; Sec. 6.2) is overstated—only the qualitative trend is supported.

The experiments validate the theory quantitatively only for small H (Fig. 3, H ≈ 0.1–3, Gaussian), but the real-data experiments operate at H ≈ 35–140, far outside the validated regime. The scaling of β with H in Fig. 4 (very gradual, slope ~-0.002 per unit H) is inconsistent with the 1/(1+H²) (or 1/(1+32H²)) dependence, indicating the H-dependence of the theory does not extrapolate to the real-data scale.

The core theory assumes i.i.d. tokens drawn from a fixed distribution ν, which does not match self-attention where queries, keys, and values are the same fixed, dependent sequence. The paper itself stresses that this dependence is 'the' key difficulty (Sec. 4) yet the analysis is i.i.d.-based; the dependence is only addressed empirically, so the central theory does not fully model the stated problem.

Framing issues: it is claimed as a contribution that the paper establishes bounds 'with smaller values of β,' but smaller β corresponds to weaker (looser) guarantees, which is confusingly presented; the sample-size condition 'n ≥ 4(1/δ−1)n^{1/8}' is self-referential and awkwardly stated.

The downstream experiment is thin (single task, 3 epochs, K = 5 Monte-Carlo repetitions, mean pooling) and the connection between attention-output rates and downstream metrics is asserted rather than derived; several presentation errors appear (e.g., push-forward notation (f_n)_♯ν_n written as '(f_n)_2ν_n', 'f_2ν'), and the text is notation-heavy.

strengths: Addresses a timely and relevant question: how attention computed on n tokens converges to its infinite-token (mean-field) limit as context length grows, which is a natural regime to study given expanding context windows.

The hardmax result (Proposition 5.5) is clean and self-contained: in the 1-D Gaussian limit, the exact logarithmic rate E|f̄_n| = ln(4)σ/(2√(2 ln n)) and E[f̄_n^2] = π²σ²/(24 ln n) are derived via Gaussian extreme-value theory, with an appealing cancellation interpretation.

The 'attention horizon' H = ||Σ^{1/2} A Σ^{1/2}||_2 is an interpretable quantity with a clean variational interpretation (largest query-key score in the covariance geometry), and the appendix contains a careful derivation showing H is the optimal B that balances the truncation/tail tradeoff.

The empirical study spans multiple models (BigBird-RoBERTa, BERT), languages (EN/DE/ZH), and datasets (Wikipedia, CC-News), plus a downstream classification task, and the windowed-sampling ablation in Appendix D goes some way toward testing robustness beyond i.i.d. subsampling.
The paper is reasonably candid in the conclusion that tightness of the upper bound (even in the Gaussian case) is open.
weaknesses: The central theoretical claims are upper bounds presented as rates. An upper bound that decays slower than 1/√n does not establish that the true rate is sub-parametric; it is fully compatible with the true rate being 1/√n. No matching lower bound is given outside the hardmax and two-Dirac examples, so the headline claim 'the rate is C'(R)/n^β with β<1/2' is not actually proven.

There is a severe quantitative mismatch between theory and experiment in the regime that matters. With the real-data horizons reported (H ~ 20-140), Theorem 5.3 predicts β = 1/(2(1+32H²)) ≈ 10⁻⁵–10⁻⁶, i.e., essentially no convergence over any practical n, whereas the experiments report β ≈ 0.25-0.5. The claim that H 'governs the rate' is therefore only qualitative; the bound is orders of magnitude loose, and the abstract's statement that real-data experiments 'support our predictions' is overstated.

Internal inconsistency about which result is being validated. The sub-Gaussian theorem uses exponent 1/(2(1+32H²)), but Figure 3 (and Props. D.5/D.23) use the Gaussian exponent 1/(2(1+H²)); the 32-fold factor is a large discrepancy that is never reconciled. It is unclear which theoretical curve the experiments are supposed to confirm.

The experimental rate estimates are unreliable: power laws are fit over n ∈ [1000, 3000], a factor of 3 in n, which is far too narrow to reliably distinguish slopes of 0.3-0.5 from 0.5, and fit uncertainty/confidence intervals are not reported. This is the primary empirical evidence for the paper's main claim.

Setup mismatch between theory and the downstream experiment: the theory assumes a single shared context of n i.i.d. tokens for all queries, while the classification experiment draws n independent keys per query and propagates through a 12-layer network. The connection between the single-layer bound and the observed downstream slowdown is therefore loose and asserted rather than demonstrated.

Presentation and consistency problems: references to 'Theorem 5.1' where Definition 5.1 is meant, inconsistent equation/result numbering (Corollary D.4 vs Theorem 5.3 vs Prop. D.23), the odd self-referential condition n ≥ 4(1/δ−1)n^{1/8}, and figure/legend mismatches (e.g., legends stating 1/(2(1+H²)) while the text discusses 32H²). These hinder verification.

Limited novelty relative to the existing mean-field/Transformer-PDE literature (Sander et al.; Geshkovski et al.; Castin et al.) and the concurrent Boursier & Boyer (2025) work on token sample complexity; the authors themselves note that Theorem 4.2's exponential-in-R constant makes the first bound 'essentially useless in practice', so the incremental contribution rests mainly on the truncation-based exponent, which is an artifact of the method and the specific constants.

The modeling choice (tokens i.i.d. from a fixed distribution, so that more context only gives a better Monte Carlo estimate of a fixed operator) may not capture why long context helps in practice, where additional tokens carry new information rather than more samples of the same law; this conceptual limitation is not discussed.

strengths: Timely, well-motivated problem: the paper formalizes 'token sample complexity' — the rate at which finite-n attention approaches its infinite-token limit — which is directly relevant to the current push toward very long contexts, and it connects this to an inference-time question (how many keys are needed to recover dense behavior).

The 'attention horizon' H = ||Σ^{1/2} A Σ^{1/2}||₂ is a genuinely useful, interpretable quantity. Remark 5.2 gives a clean geometric interpretation (largest query-key score in the covariance unit ball), and the horizon-dependent exponent β(H) is supported both theoretically (Thm 5.3, Prop D.23) and empirically (Fig. 3, Fig. 4, Fig. 5).

The technical machinery is substantial and appropriate: since the softmax kernel e^{⟨Ax,y⟩} is not uniformly Lipschitz and the self-attention setting couples queries, keys, and values, standard uniform CLTs do not apply; the use of symmetrization, Dudley's entropy integral with a duality argument for the vector-valued process, and sub-Gaussian tail control is a real contribution (Section 4.3, Appendix C).

The hardmax analysis (Prop 5.5) is a nice result: the exact 1/√(ln n) rate and the explicit 'cancellation' mechanism for symmetric Gaussians (max/min selected with ~equal probability) is a clean and somewhat surprising asymptotics, and Remark 5.6/Appendix C.9 correctly show sub-Gaussianity is necessary via a heavy-tailed counterexample.

The empirical validation is broad: synthetic Gaussian (low and high dimension, Fig. 3, 7), non-Gaussian sub-Gaussian (Fig. 8), real text across languages and sources with BigBird and BERT (Fig. 4, 5, 9, 10), structured windowed sampling (Fig. 11), and an end-to-end arxiv-classification experiment (Fig. 2, 6). The stratification by horizon is a thoughtful way to connect theory to downstream behavior.

The paper is honest about limitations: it explicitly states that tightness of the upper bound is open, discusses the i.i.d. assumption and its mismatch with structured sampling, and clearly delineates its differences from concurrent work (Boursier & Boyer, 2025).
weaknesses: The central theoretical model — n i.i.d. tokens drawn from a fixed distribution ν — does not match real token sequences, which are strongly correlated and non-stationary. Since 'token sample complexity' is defined in this i.i.d. regime, the bridge from the theorems to 'how many tokens an LLM needs' is indirect. The windowed-sampling experiments are a useful partial remedy but are not covered by the theory.

The headline general bound (Thm 5.3, β = 1/(2(1+32H²))) is loose relative to the Gaussian special case (Prop D.23, β = 1/(2(1+H²))), and it is the latter — not the main theorem — that matches the experiments. The factor 32 in the general exponent is not shown to be sharp, so the quantitative claim in the abstract ('C'(R)/n^β with β<1/2 … matching real-data behavior') is validated for a special case rather than for the stated general result.

All results are upper bounds; no lower bounds establish tightness in the general sub-Gaussian setting. The paper's statement that the bound 'describes the observed slow convergence rate on real data' rests on empirical fitting, not on a matching lower bound. The polylog prefactor P(√ln n) is also never disentangled from the power law in the fits.

The claim that the attention-output slowdown 'propagates through the full network' to downstream quality is supported only by correlation (Fig. 2, 6). The deep-composition result (Cor. D.7) assumes i.i.d. subsampling at every layer, which does not correspond to the actual experiment (per-query key sampling at inference); the propagation claim is therefore not theoretically justified by the experiment that is meant to support it.

The empirical rate estimates come from log-log linear fits over fairly narrow ranges of n (e.g., 1000–3000, or 64–4096), where polylog factors, crossover behavior (explicitly noted near the hardmax transition in Fig. 3), and the choice of fit window can bias the fitted exponent. Main-text figures report point exponents with little discussion of fit sensitivity or goodness-of-fit, which weakens the quantitative agreement between theory and data.

Presentation and notation have rough edges: dimension conventions shift between k, d, and p (Definition 3.1 uses Q,K,V ∈ R^{k×d} with f_n : R^d → R^k, later V ∈ R^{p×d}); the 1/√k scaling and the distinction between Ā and A are easy to lose; and the condition 'n ≥ 4(1/δ − 1) n^{1/8}' in Thm 5.3 is stated in a self-referential, confusing way.

Novelty relative to concurrent work is modest. The authors' stated differentiators (self-attention dependence, smaller β, hardmax asymptotics) are real, but the core object — convergence of finite-token attention to a mean-field limit — is shared with Boursier & Boyer (2025), and the incremental gain is mostly in the constant/exponent of an upper bound rather than a qualitatively new phenomenon.
